# The 1840 census residue

*Generated by `tools/report_census_1840_residue.py --write` from
`data/research/census_1840/residue_1840.json` and the committed page files.*
*Do not hand-edit: `--check` compares this file against a fresh derivation, and
every figure below is read out of the tree rather than typed into the source.*

**What this is.** The 1840 federal census is CLOSED for the purposes of the 1835
reconstruction, and this is the residue it closed with: every reading that did not
settle, the leaf it is on, the readings that compete for it, and why it stayed open.
A stated gap is a finished answer; a leaf-by-leaf programme of single-column
adjudications is not one, and eight tickets of it were what this replaced.

**No residue row may be refiled as a ticket.** This is T-1290 acceptance 4, and it is what keeps a closed programme closed: a row below is a stated gap, not a backlog item. A row that later blocks real reconstruction work is reopened by the ticket it blocks, and by nothing else.

## What the residue does to the 1835 town

One sentence per class, and the first four of them are the same sentence for the
same reason.

**A footing that does not close** — None. A column that closes at one figure rather than another moves no 1835 card: the 1840 census is five years after the scene, and the carry rule under which any of it reaches a person — LATER EVIDENCE ONLY, never back-projected to 1835-07-01 — makes a household's size in 1840 a bracket on a household other sources already placed, never a figure the scene reads.

**A figure the exposure lost** — None. Both rows are footings of the SCHOOLS block, which counts scholars and illiterates in 1840 and seats, dates or names nobody in 1835.

**A two-stroke figure the leaf fixes nowhere else** — None. Both rows are age-and-sex tallies within a household of 1840. They change a household's shape five years after the scene, which the carry rule already forbids reaching an 1835 card.

**Ink no pass has committed** — None that is known, and this is the one class where that sentence is a judgement rather than a derivation: unread ink cannot be shown to say nothing. What bounds it is that these are 1840 leaves, that the 1835 layer cites none of them, and that nothing in the 1840 schedule seats a person, dates an arrival or names a trade in 1835 even when it is read.

**A leaf the tool cannot read** — None directly — it costs reading time, not truth. It is the reason the unread leaves above are priced one per run, and it is the one row here a later reconstruction ticket might actually want fixed.

### The same claim, put to the tree

`head_spend_1835.json` is the record of what the 1840 census actually wrote onto an
1835 card. Its carry rule is LATER EVIDENCE ONLY: an 1839 or 1840 appearance alone
is never an 1835 resident, and 1840 household composition is never back-projected to
the 1835-07-01 scene.

| | |
|---|---|
| heads adjudicated in the 1840 crosswalk | 965 |
| rulings that reach a person at all | 30 |
| 1835 grades the whole of the 1840 census changed | **0** |
| distinct leaves those rulings cite | 18 |
| leaves this residue stands on | 8 |
| leaves in both sets | **0** |

**They do not intersect.** No leaf carrying a residue row is cited by any of the
30 people the 1840 census wrote to, so the residue could be
settled either way tomorrow without moving a card — and the grade count says the
same thing from the other side: five years after the scene, the census moved none.

**Where it very nearly does touch — `33S7-9YYJ-PC`.** Row 2's footing is the page-population key that holds 33S7-9YYJ-L3's refusal to pair with 33S7-9YYJ-PC, and PC is among the leaves the 1835 spend cites. The adjacency is real and it is narrow: what the 1835 layer takes off PC is a head's name and line, which no pairing key touches, and a pairing that moved would change which continuation sheet PC's tallies belong to rather than who stood on it. It is named here so that a later ticket blocked by the pairing knows where to look.
